analysis.one_liner: Forces the EPA to tighten lead-paint dust standards and verify cleanup with real dust testing to protect pregnant women and children.
analysis.headline: The Senate environment committee reported the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in September 2008, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2001 the EPA set limits for how much lead dust could remain on floors and window sills, and its 2008 renovation rule let cleaners verify their work with a simple 'white cloth' wipe. EPA's own science advisory panel said those limits were obsolete and the verification method unreliable, because newer research showed lead harms children even below the old thresholds. This bill would have ordered the EPA to rewrite the dust standard using the best current science, require independent dust testing to confirm homes were actually clean after renovations, publish results to owners and occupants, and fund free lead-safe work training for low-income workers. It cleared the Senate environment committee and was placed on the Senate's calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant women and young children living in or around pre-1978 housing, where lead-based paint was still legal; the bill itself notes EPA's estimate that roughly 310,000 U.S. children ages 1-5 had blood-lead levels above 10 micrograms per deciliter, and that low-income and minority children face the highest risk. Low-income workers would also have gained access to free, certified lead-safe work training under the grant program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and pregnant women in older housing

how_it_helps.text: It directed the EPA to replace 2001-era dust limits (40 micrograms per square foot on floors, 250 on window sills) with a stricter standard reflecting post-1991 studies showing harm to children below 10 micrograms of lead per deciliter of blood.

It would have replaced the 'white cloth' wipe test — which EPA's own science advisory panel called simplistic and unreliable — with lab-based dust sampling and clearance by an independent certified assessor after renovation work.

It required a written report to owners and occupants describing what hazard-reduction steps were taken and what the test results showed, and required a trained, certified worker to be present at all times during covered work.

It created a grant program, authorized at $7 million for fiscal years 2009-2012, to pay for no-cost, culturally and linguistically appropriate lead-safe training, with priority for low-income workers.
It required EPA to re-evaluate the hazard standard at least every five years and tighten it whenever new science showed greater dangers to pregnant women and children.

analysis.who_pays: Renovation and painting contractors working on pre-1978 homes, who would bear the cost of independent clearance testing, stricter work practices, and keeping a trained certified worker on site; some of that cost would flow to landlords and homeowners as higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Requiring an independent certified assessor to clear every renovation, plus a trained and certified worker on site at all times, adds real cost to painting and remodeling work in pre-1978 housing, which would ultimately be passed through to homeowners and landlords in higher prices.

The bill authorized only $7 million over fiscal years 2009-2012 for its training grant program, a modest sum against the nationwide need to train and certify enough workers and sampling technicians to staff every covered job site.

The deadlines were aggressive — updated renovation rules within 90 days of enactment and a revised hazard standard by April 30, 2009 — which regulators and affected firms could reasonably have argued left too little time for notice, comment, and transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — cutting children's and pregnant women's lead exposure from renovation dust using standards current science supports — is large and one-sided: lead poisoning causes permanent developmental harm, and the bill's costs fall mostly on renovation firms as testing and work-practice changes, partly offset by authorized training grants. The design has weak points: the mandated deadlines were tight, $7 million over four years was modest for a national training push, and the independent-clearance requirement could add expense to smaller jobs, some of which would be passed to homeowners through prices. On balance, the protective benefits outweighed those costs, but the bill never got far enough for Congress or the public to debate and refine them.

outcome.mechanism: The committee wrote and reported the bill and it was placed on the Senate's waiting list for floor action, but the Senate never voted on it and the Congress ran out of time on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee ordered an original measure reported on September 17, 2008, and Senator Boxer formally reported it on September 26 with written report 110-515, including additional views from some members.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 1097), the waiting list for floor action, on September 26, 2008.
No further action was taken; the Senate never voted on the bill, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with the measure still on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renovation firms came out ahead: they avoided independent clearance testing, stricter work practices, and the certified-worker-on-site requirement, and EPA remained free to keep the 2001 dust standards and the 'white cloth' verification method its own science advisers had called obsolete. Children and pregnant women in older housing continued to face the weaker standards.

for.name: Senator Barbara Boxer
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced and reported the bill as an original committee measure and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the original measure reported on September 17, 2008, issuing written report 110-515, with additional views filed.

against.name: Environmental Protection Agency (Bush administration)
against.what_they_did: Promulgated the 2001 lead hazard standards and the 2008 renovation rule that the bill's findings say relied on cleaning practices and the 'white cloth' verification method its own science advisers had criticized as inadequate and inaccurate — the rules this bill would have forced the agency to strengthen.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill; the committee report noted additional views filed, but the record shows no partisan breakdown.

industries.industry: Renovation, repair, and painting contractors working on pre-1978 housing
industries.note: The bill would have required independent post-work clearance testing by a certified assessor, HUD-level work practices, and a certified worker on site at all times — ongoing compliance costs that firms doing this work avoided under the 2008 rule. Firms that failed random sampling would have had to pay for clearance on every subsequent job.

industries.industry: Environmental testing, risk assessment, and lead-training services
industries.note: Independent clearance by certified assessors and sampling technicians, plus grant-funded training expansion, would have created steady demand for lead dust testing and for accredited training and certification providers.

industries.industry: Landlords and owners of older rental housing
industries.note: Owners would face recleaning and clearance costs when renovations exceeded standards, but would also receive a written record of hazard-reduction work and test results, and tenants — often their customers — would face less lead dust exposure.
